question_text: Keshan disease is a cardiomyopathy, first identified in China. It occurs as due to eating of food produced from soil deficient of which of the following minerals?
explanation:
Option A:

  • Zinc deficiency can lead to Acrodermatitis enteropathica.
  • Zinc Deficiency can also lead to stunted growth in children, loss of taste sensation, poor wound healing, skin lesions (hyperkeratosis, dermatitis), alopecia, impaired spermatogenesis seen.
  • It can also lead to depression, dementia and other psychiatric disorders.
  • Acrodermatitis Enteropathica:Genetic condition where zinc absorption is defective which lead to zinc deficiency.
    • It is characterized by acrodermatitis (inflammation around mouth, nose, fingers etc), diarrhoea, alopecia (loss of hair in discrete areas), ophthalmoplegia and hypogonadism

Option B:

  • Selenium deficiency can lead to Keshan disease.
  • It is prevalent in Keshan province in China, soil is deficient in selenium.
  • Leads to cardiac problems like myocardial necrosis, cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac enlargement, cardiomyopathy etc
  • Isolated selenium deficiency in other parts of world causes liver necrosis, cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy and muscular dystrophy.

Option C:

  • Iodine deficiency can lead to goitre. Goitre is an enlargement of thyroid gland.
  • It occurs as a part of compensation for decreased synthesis of thyroid hormones (Associated with elevated TSH).
  • It is also due to a failure in auto regulation of T3 & T4 synthesis, caused by deficiency or excess of iodide
  • It is more common in women & with increased age

Causes of Goitre

  • Endemic: in some parts of India (Himalaya belt) & S. Asia & America. This is due to iodine deficiency in the diet. Such geographical regions usually away from sea coast where water & soil are low in iodine content.
  • Relative deficiency during adolescence, pregnancy, lactation etc due to higher requirement which may not be fulfilled nutritionally
  • Goitrogens (Goitrogenic substances)- Substances that interfere with production of thyroid hormones by blocking absorption or utilization of iodine and lead to goitre
    • Include thiocyanates, nitrates, perchlorates, drugs like thiourea, thiouracil, thiocarbamide etc.
    • Plant foods like cabbage, cauliflower, turnip, peanuts, soybeans contain goitrogens (thiocyanates)

Clinical features of Goitre

  • It is usually asymptomatic
  • Enlargement of thyroid gland (neck swelling), Acute pain from thyroidal haemorrhage, Dysphagia (trouble swallowing), Dyspnea (trouble breathing)
  • It may lead to hypothyroidism
  • Severe iodine deficiency during pregnancy and early child growth lead to CRETINISM.
  • It can lead to mental retardation, short stature, hypothyroidism etc

Treatment of Goitre

  • Iodine supplementation, repletion must be done slowly to prevent hyperthyroidism
  • Hypothyroidism is treated with thyroid hormone supplementation
  • Thyroidectomy may be required in symptomatic cases
  • Prevention by iodine supplementation (e.g., iodized salt) in endemic area

Option D:

  • Fluoride deficiency can lead to dental carries.
  • Drinking water containing less than 0.5 ppm of fluoride is associated with development of dental caries in children.

Reference: Lippincott Illustrate Reviews Biochemistry 8th edition (South Asian edition) CH 33 PN 561

question_text: Which of the following micronutrients is associated with decreased sexual maturation and hypogonadism?
explanation:
Explanation:

Zinc is an essential trace element crucial for normal growth, sexual maturation, and gonadal function. Deficiency in zinc is associated with delayed sexual development and hypogonadism due to its role in hormone synthesis and reproductive system regulation.

  • Zinc deficiency can impair the release and action of gonadotropins and testosterone.
  • Zinc plays a role in spermatogenesis and testicular development.
  • Other micronutrients like copper, selenium, and iron are essential for general health but are not directly linked to hypogonadism or delayed sexual maturation.

Explanation of other options:

question_text: Which of the following acts as a major intracellular antioxidant and helps in detoxifying reactive oxygen species?
explanation:
Explanation:

Among the given options, the major intracellular antioxidant that helps in detoxifying reactive oxygen species is glutathione.

  • Antioxidants function to control and limit lipid peroxidation. Synthetic antioxidants like propyl gallate, BHA, and BHT are commonly added to foods.
  • Natural antioxidants include lipid-soluble vitamin E (tocopherol) and water-soluble compounds such as urate and vitamin C. β-Carotene also acts as an antioxidant under low oxygen tension.

Antioxidants are categorised into two types:

  1. Preventive antioxidants: slow down the initiation of free radical chain reactions. Examples are catalase, glutathione peroxidase, selenium (a component of glutathione peroxidase), and metal ion chelators such as EDTA and DTPA.
  2. Chain-breaking antioxidants: stop the propagation of free radical reactions. Examples include superoxide dismutase, which removes superoxide radicals in aqueous environments, and compounds like urate and vitamin E, which block lipid-phase radicals.
    • Enzymes that generate and use superoxide are mainly located in peroxisomes, where they occur alongside superoxide dismutase, catalase, and different peroxidases. These enzymes play a role in converting hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. (Options B and C ruled out)
    • Reduced glutathione eliminates hydrogen peroxide by participating in a reaction catalysed by glutathione peroxidase, an enzyme that relies on selenocysteine (a selenium-containing form of cysteine) at its active site. It acts as a key intracellular antioxidant and reducing agent, ensuring that vital enzyme sulfhydryl (SH) groups remain in their reduced, active form.

Explanation of other options:

Myeloperoxidase (Option D): Myeloperoxidase is an enzyme found in neutrophils that uses hydrogen peroxide and chloride ions to generate hypochlorous acid (bleach), hypochlorite, and chlorine. These highly reactive products play an important role in killing and halogenating microorganisms and tumour cells. However, if not properly regulated, they can also damage host tissues.

question_text: Wilson's disease is due to a defect in copper transport. It is caused due to a mutation of which gene?
explanation:
Explanation:

Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13. This gene encodes a copper-transporting P-type ATPase, which is primarily expressed in the liver. The defective ATP7B protein impairs the incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin and, more critically, prevents the biliary excretion of excess copper. This leads to toxic accumulation of copper in the liver, brain (particularly the basal ganglia), corneas (causing Kayser-Fleischer rings), and other organs.

Explanation of other options:

HNF 1 Alpha (Option A): Mutations in the HNF1α gene are associated with Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY) type 3.

Fibrillin (Option C): Mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene (FBN1) are the cause of Marfan syndrome.

COL1A1 (Option D): Mutations in the COL1A1 or COL1A2 genes are responsible for various forms of Osteogenesis Imperfecta.

Key Takeaways:

  • Wilson's disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene.
  • This leads to copper accumulation in the liver and brain, causing hepatic and neuropsychiatric symptoms.

question_text: All of the following mechanism can be used to intercept damaging done by Reactive Oxygen species (ROS) and slowing ageing, except:
explanation:
Option A:

  • In the cytoplasm, the cysteine-containing tripeptide glutathione acts as a chemical redox protectant that reacts directly with ROS to generate less reactive compounds such as water.
  • Oxidized glutathione, which consists of two tripeptides linked by an S-S bond, is then enzymatically reduced to maintain the pool of protectant.
  • Glutathione can also react directly with cysteine sulfenic acids and disulfides on proteins to restore them to their reduced state, and form adducts with toxic xenobiotics.
  • Ascorbic acid and vitamin E also possess antioxidant properties, which accounts for the popularity of diets that emphasize foods rich in these compounds, or supplementation with them, to combat ROS and, hopefully, slow aging.

Option B & Option D:

  • Enzymes such as superoxide dismutase and catalase protect the cell by converting superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, respectively to less reactive products thereby preventing potential molecular damage before it occurs.
  • For examples fruit flies that have been genetically altered to express elevated levels of superoxide dismutase exhibit significantly extended life span.

Option C:

  • Caspases are not involved in neutralizing ROS, but involved in apoptosis.
  • Apoptosis is a genetically directed program, which when activated, causes cell death. The main proteins involved in apoptosis are proteolytic enzymes termed caspases that normally exist in inactive forms, the procaspases.
  • The name caspase is derived from the fact that these enzymes utilize an active site cysteine to cleave polypeptide chains immediately after aspartic residues.
  • About 15 human caspases are known, although not all participate in apoptosis. When those involved in apoptosis are activated (mainly caspases 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10), they participate in a cascade of events that ultimately kills cells by digesting various proteins and other molecules.

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 57 PN 713

question_text: Menke's disease is due to a deficiency of:
explanation:
Explanation:

Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7A gene. This gene encodes a copper-transporting ATPase essential for the absorption of copper from the intestines and its distribution across the blood-brain barrier. The defect leads to a systemic copper deficiency despite adequate dietary intake, as copper becomes trapped in intestinal cells.

The deficiency of copper-dependent enzymes (e.g., lysyl oxidase, cytochrome c oxidase) results in the characteristic symptoms:

  • Kinky hair (failure in collagen cross linkage)
  • Hypotonia
  • Neurodegeneration
  • Connective tissue abnormalities.

Explanation of other options:
Zinc (Option A): Zinc deficiency causes acrodermatitis enteropathica, not Menkes disease.

Iron (Option C): Iron deficiency causes microcytic hypochromic anemia.

Magnesium (Option D): Magnesium deficiency causes neuromuscular irritability and cardiac arrhythmias.

Key Takeaways:

  • Menkes disease is an X-linked disorder of copper absorption leading to systemic copper deficiency.
  • It is characterized by kinky hair and severe neurological deterioration.

question_text: Which one of the following is negative acute phase protein?
explanation:
Option B: Transthyretin also known as prealbumin, which level is decreased during inflammation, so termed as negative acute phase proteins.

Option A, Option C & Option D: Ferritin, Ceruloplasmin, Haptoglobin are positive acute phase proteins, which level is increased during inflammation.

Acute Phase Proteins

  • Those plasma proteins which levels are changed in plasma (> 25%) during inflammations(as result of any infection, injury, malignancy, surgery etc) are known as Acute Phase Proteins or Acute Phase Reactants.
  • Such Acute phase response is nonspecific response and associated with a characteristic pattern of changes in such proteins
  • Some mediators like cytokines (IL-1, IL-6), tumor necrosis factors α and β, Interferons, platelet activating factor etc, causes change in such proteins level.

I) Positive Acute Phase Proteins

Plasma proteins which levels increase in Inflammation (increase upto 50 to 1000 folds)

Examples: 1-antitypsin, 2-macroglobulin, C-reactive protein, Complement proteins, Ceruloplasmin, Haptoglobin, Ferritin, Fibrinogen, Mannose binding proteins

Their synthesis is increased as body's response to injury or inflammation.

Functions of these proteins: Help in inflammatory reaction & fight against infection and maintain homeostasis like Binding to polysaccharides in bacterial walls, Activate complement system, Stimulate phagocytosis, prevents damage done by proteolytic enzymes, Repair damaged tissues

C - reactive protein (CRP)

  • Major acute phase proteins
  • Beta globulin, MW is 115 - 140 kD
  • C strands for carbohydrate to which it binds on the capsule of pneumococci
  • It involves in promotion of immune system through activation of complement cascade
  • Produced in liver and is present in circulation in minute concentration (<1 mg/dl)
  • Estimation of CRP in serum is important for the evaluation of acute phase responseduring inflammations. It increases when inflammation is aggressive & decreaseswhen inflammation subsides.
  • Preferred over ESR as changes reflected earlier.
  • High sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) level in blood has a positive correlation in predicting risk of coronary artery diseases.

II) Negative Acute Phase Proteins

Plasma proteins which levels are decrease in inflammation

Examples: Albumin, Prealbumin (Transthyretin), Transferrin, Retinol binding proteins

  • Synthesis of these proteins decrease to save amino acids for synthesis of positive acute phase proteins
  • Acute phase proteins help to monitor inflammatory response eg CRP & Ferritin are used to monitor Covid infection

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 31st edition CH 52 PN 630 Change reference to 32nd edition.

question_text: A 37-year-old male presents with bleeding gums, petechiae and anemia. The doctor diagnosed him with scurvy. Which of the following Vitamin deficiency leads to scurvy?
explanation:
Pantothenic acid deficiency leads to dermatitis, enteritis, nutritional melalgia (burning foot syndrome), alopecia. Folic acid deficiency leads to neural tube defects in children born to folate deficient woman. Biotin deficiency leads to dermatitis, enteritis, hallucinations.

Option C: Ascorbic acid deficiency leads to scurvy.

Option A: (Pantothenic acid): Involved in energy metabolism, but its deficiency does not cause scurvy.

Option B: (Folic acid): Essential for DNA synthesis and red blood cell formation; its deficiency can cause anaemia but not scurvy.

Option D: (Biotin): Important for fatty acid metabolism and glucose production; deficiency leads to skin issues and hair loss, not scurvy.

Key takeaways:

Pantothenic acid, folic acid, and biotin deficiencies cause dermatitis and other issues, while ascorbic acid deficiency specifically leads to scurvy.

question_text: A patient presented to the OPD with liver damage. The picture depicts the patient’s eyes. Which of the following subsequent factors is responsible for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective copper metabolism.
  • Copper gradually accumulates in the liver, brain, cornea, kidney, and joints, leading to progressive organ damage.
  • The hallmark laboratory profile is low serum ceruloplasmin, increased hepatic copper content, and elevated urinary copper excretion.

Gene Involved

  • Caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene (chromosome 13).
  • ATP7B encodes a copper-transporting ATPase in hepatocytes that normally facilitates copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and biliary excretion.

Pathogenesis

  • Genetic mutation → defective ATP7B protein.
  • Biliary excretion of copper is impaired → copper trapped in hepatocytes.
  • Progressive copper overload in liver → oxidative injury, lipid peroxidation, and hepatocellular damage.
  • When hepatic storage capacity is exceeded → free copper leaks into circulation.
  • Systemic distribution and deposition:
    • Brain (basal ganglia): Neurological and psychiatric features.
    • Cornea: Deposition at Descemet's membrane → Kayser-Fleischer rings.
    • Kidneys: Tubular dysfunction, hematuria, aminoaciduria.
    • Bones/Joints: Premature osteoarthritis and arthropathy.

Mechanism of Tissue Injury:

  • Copper excess causes:
    • Oxidative stress
    • Enzyme inhibition
    • Lipid peroxidation of cell membranes
  • These lead to cell death and fibrosis.

Explanation of other options:

Glucose (Option B): A carbohydrate fuel, not implicated in Wilson's disease.

Galactose (Option C): Its accumulation occurs in galactosemia, not Wilson's.

Mannose (Option D): Involved in glycoprotein synthesis, unrelated to copper metabolism.

question_text: The subcellular organelle which is associated with killing of viruses and bacteria is?
explanation:
Explanation:

The lysosome is the primary organelle responsible for the intracellular degradation and killing of pathogens like viruses and bacteria. This process occurs within specialized immune cells such as macrophages and neutrophils. After a pathogen is engulfed by phagocytosis, forming a phagosome, this vesicle fuses with a lysosome to create a phagolysosome. The lysosome contains a powerful cocktail of hydrolytic enzymes (e.g., proteases, nucleases, lipases) and maintains an acidic pH, which collectively digest and destroy the engulfed microorganism.

Explanation of other options:

Peroxisome (Option A): Peroxisomes are involved in beta-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids and the detoxification of reactive oxygen species (e.g., using catalase). They are not primarily involved in pathogen destruction.

Mitochondria (Option B): Mitochondria are the "powerhouses" of the cell, generating ATP through oxidative phosphorylation. They play a role in apoptosis but not in the direct enzymatic degradation of pathogens.

Golgi apparatus (Option D): The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins for secretion or delivery to other organelles. It is part of the cellular trafficking system but does not have a direct role in killing pathogens.

Key Takeaways:

  • Lysosomes are the digestive organelles of the cell, crucial for the destruction of phagocytosed pathogens.
  • The fusion of a phagosome with a lysosome forms a phagolysosome, where degradation occurs.

question_text: A young man met with a motor bike accident and had injury to ileum and jejunum. Therefore, the entire ileum and partial jejunum was resected. Which of the following is the patient most likely to suffer from:
explanation:
Option A: Vitamin B12 is absorbed bound to intrinsic factor, a small glycoprotein secreted by the parietal cells of the gastric mucosa. Gastric acid and pepsin release the vitamin from protein binding in food and make it available to bind to cobalophilin, a binding protein secreted in the saliva. In the duodenum, cobalophilin is hydrolyzed, releasing the vitamin for binding to intrinsic factors. Pancreatic insufficiency can therefore be a factor in the development of vitamin B12 deficiency, resulting in the excretion of cobalophilin-bound vitamin B12. Intrinsic factor binds only the active vitamin B12 vitamers and not other corrinoids. Vitamin B12 is absorbed from the distal third of the ileum via receptors that bind the intrinsic factor–vitamin B12 complex, but not free intrinsic factor or free vitamin. There is considerable enterohepatic circulation of vitamin B12, with excretion in the bile, then reabsorption after binding to intrinsic factor in the ileum.

So for those patients in which ileum and partial jejunum was resected, vitamin B12 deficiency is very common.

Option B, Option C & Option D: Constipation, Gastric Ulcer & Diarrhoea usually not associated with vitamin B12 deficiency.

question_text: Iron absorption is limited and strictly regulated due to:
option_a: Non enzymatic generation of free radical by iron salt
option_d: Due to limited quantity of iron in food
explanation:
Option A:

  • H2O2lead to only minimal tissue damage, when compared to other free radicals.
  • But in the presence of free irons, H2O2 can generate OH (hydroxyl radical) which is highly reactive.

  • Free radicals can damage cell and tissue.
  • Hence to reduce the risk of adverse effects of nonenzymic generation of free radicals by iron salts, absorption is strictly regulated.

Option B:

  • Iron homeostasis is maintained by regulation at the level of absorption.
  • When iron stores in body are depleted, absorption is enhanced.
  • When adequate quantity of iron is stored, absorption is decreased. This is referred to as “mucosal block” of regulation of absorption of iron.
  • So excess intake of iron will never lead to iron overload (hemochromatosis).
  • It can occur when repeated blood transfusion given to patients or hereditary.

Option C: Iron absorption is complex, but this is not the reason which is responsible for its strict regulation.

Option D: Diet contain large quantity of iron, but its absorption is limited. Only ~10% of dietary iron is absorbed, and only 1 to 5% from many plant foods.

Reference: Harper’s illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 44 PN 523

question_text:
Identify the image and choose the correct answer related to it.

A. Eyes open, person is able to walk.
B. Eyes closed, the person falls down.
option_a: It shows positive Romberg's sign due to vitamin B12 deficiency.
option_b: It shows positive Babinski's sign due to vitamin B12 deficiency.
option_c: It shows positive Chvostek's sign due to calcium deficiency.
option_d: It shows positive Trousseau's sign due to calcium deficiency.
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The Romberg test assesses proprioception, or the body's sense of spatial orientation.
  • In the Romberg test, the patient stands with feet together and eyes open, then closes their eyes.
  • A positive Romberg sign is observed if the person becomes unsteady and sways or falls when their eyes are closed, indicating sensory ataxia. This can be due to vitamin B12 deficiency, which affects the dorsal columns of the spinal cord responsible for proprioception.

question_text: Which of the following sentence is true regarding secretion and action of hepcidin?
explanation:
• Expression of the ferroportin gene (and possibly also that for the divalent metal ion transporter) is downregulated by hepcidin, a peptide secreted by the liver when body iron reserves are adequate.
  • In response to hypoxia, anemia, or haemorrhage, the synthesis of hepcidin is reduced, leading to increased synthesis of ferroportin and increased iron absorption.

Option A: Hepcidin does not upregulate the ferroportin gene

Option B: Hepcidin downregulates the ferroportin gene, so there’s a reduced synthesis of ferroportin and hence, decreased iron absorption.

Option C: Hepcidin decreases iron absorption.

Option D: Synthesis of hepcidin is reduced during hypoxia, anemia and haemorrhage.

Reference: Harper’s illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 44 PN 523
